derivations.claim: Let $x=\sqrt{m^2-Q^2}$. By [F6] and [A1], $0<x\le m$, so $r_-=m-x\ge0$ and $r_+=m+x>0$. Factoring gives $f(r)=(r-r_+)(r-r_-)/r^2>0$ on $r>r_+$. From [F1]–[F2] the equatorial metric components are $g_{00}=-f$, $g_{rr}=f^{-1}$, $g_{\theta\theta}=r^2$, and $g_{\phi\phi}=r^2\sin^2\theta$. Substitution in [F5] gives $\Gamma^0{}_{0r}=f'/(2f)$, $\Gamma^\phi{}_{r\phi}=1/r$, $\Gamma^r{}_{00}=ff'/2$, $\Gamma^r{}_{rr}=-f'/(2f)$, $\Gamma^r{}_{\phi\phi}=-fr\sin^2\theta$, $\Gamma^r{}_{\theta\theta}=-fr$, $\Gamma^\theta{}_{r\theta}=1/r$, and $\Gamma^\theta{}_{\phi\phi}=-\sin\theta\cos\theta$. The $x^0$ and $\phi$ geodesic equations of [F4] are therefore $\ddot x^0+(f'/f)\dot r\dot x^0=0$ and $\ddot\phi+2(\dot r/r)\dot\phi=0$. At $\theta=\pi/2$, $\dot\theta=0$, the $r$ equation is $\ddot r+\tfrac12ff'(\dot x^0)^2-\tfrac{f'}{2f}\dot r^2-fr\dot\phi^2=0$. The $\theta$ equation is $\ddot\theta+2(\dot r/r)\dot\theta-\sin\theta\cos\theta\dot\phi^2=0$, so $\theta=\pi/2$, $\dot\theta=0$ is invariant. Differentiating the $x^0$ and $\phi$ equations shows that $E:=f\dot x^0$ and $\ell:=r^2\dot\phi$ are constant along the geodesic.
The null condition is $-f(\dot x^0)^2+f^{-1}\dot r^2+r^2\dot\phi^2=0$. Multiplying by $f>0$ and using the constants from 1.1 gives $\dot r^2+\ell^2h(r)=E^2$, where $h=f/r^2$.

For a circular orbit $r=r_c$, the radial geodesic equation from 1.1 has $\dot r=\ddot r=0$ and reads $\tfrac12ff'(\dot x^0)^2-fr_c(\dot\phi)^2=0$. The null equation and $\ell\ne0$ imply $r_cf'(r_c)-2f(r_c)=0$, equivalently $h'(r_c)=0$. Direct differentiation gives $h'(r)=-2(r^2-3mr+2Q^2)/r^5$, so its algebraic roots are $r_{\mathrm{ph}\pm}=(3m\pm\sqrt{9m^2-8Q^2})/2$. They are real because $9m^2-8Q^2=m^2+8(m^2-Q^2)>0$.

Put $x=\sqrt{m^2-Q^2}$, so $0<x\le m$. Then $\sqrt{9m^2-8Q^2}=\sqrt{m^2+8x^2}>x$, and
$$r_{\mathrm{ph}+}-r_+=\frac{m+\sqrt{m^2+8x^2}-2x}{2}=\frac{(m-x)+(\sqrt{m^2+8x^2}-x)}2>0.$$
For $Q^2>0$, [F3] identifies $r_+$ as the outer local horizon. For $Q^2=0$, [F1] gives $f=1-2m/r$, whose larger root is $r_+=2m$; the same inequality applies. Thus $f(r_{\mathrm{ph}+})>0$ and the outer root lies in the static exterior.
At the outer root, $r^2-3mr+2Q^2=0$ and $2r_{\mathrm{ph}+}-3m=\sqrt{9m^2-8Q^2}$, so $h''(r_{\mathrm{ph}+})=-2\sqrt{9m^2-8Q^2}/r_{\mathrm{ph}+}^5<0$. Hence $h$ has a strict local maximum there.

Since $f(r_{\mathrm{ph}+})>0$, [F6] defines $\sqrt{h(r_{\mathrm{ph}+})}$. Choose $\ell>0$ and $E=\ell\sqrt{h(r_{\mathrm{ph}+})}$. citations.quote: Fix $L>0$ and take the extremal RN datum with $M=q_e=L$, $q_m=0$, on $r>L$ in [[def-emg-xs-rn-data]]. For each dimensionless $\lambda>0$, define $$\Phi_\lambda(T,R,\omega)=(x^0=T/\lambda,\ r=L+\lambda R,\ \omega),\qquad (T,R,\omega)\in\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)\times S^2.$$

derivations.claim: The extremality identity gives $f(r)=(1-m/r)^2=\lambda^2R^2/(m+\lambda R)^2$. The map $\Phi_\lambda$ is a diffeomorphism from $D$ onto $\mathbb R_{x^0}\times(m,\infty)_r\times S^2$, with inverse $T=\lambda x^0$, $R=(r-m)/\lambda$. Its differentials satisfy $dx^0=dT/\lambda$ and $dr=\lambda dR$. Substitution in [F1] gives the displayed $g_\lambda$.
The same pullback differentials give $dx^0\wedge dr=(dT/\lambda)\wedge(\lambda dR)=dT\wedge dR$; substituting $r=m+\lambda R$ in the two-form of [F1] gives the displayed $\mathcal F_\lambda$.

Fix a compact $K\subset D$ and choose $0<\delta\le R\le B<\infty$ on its radial projection. For $A_\lambda(R)=(m+\lambda R)^{-2}$ and each integer $j\ge0$,
$$\partial_R^jA_\lambda(R)=(-1)^j(j+1)!\,\frac{\lambda^j}{(m+\lambda R)^{j+2}}.$$
The denominator is at least $m^{j+2}$; for $j=0$, $A_\lambda\to m^{-2}$ uniformly on $[\delta,B]$, and for $j\ge1$ the displayed derivatives tend uniformly to zero. Thus every radial derivative of $R^2A_\lambda$ converges uniformly to that of $R^2/m^2$. The other radial metric coefficient is $m^2R^{-2}+2m\lambda R^{-1}+\lambda^2$, and the angular coefficient is $m^2+2m\lambda R+\lambda^2R^2$; all their derivatives converge uniformly on $[\delta,B]$. The electric field coefficient is $-q_eA_\lambda$, and the magnetic term is independent of $\lambda$. The fixed smooth sphere tensors have bounded derivatives on compact subsets of each chart in a finite atlas covering the sphere projection of $K$. Therefore every coordinate derivative of every coefficient of $g_\lambda$ and $\mathcal F_\lambda$ converges uniformly on $K$ to the displayed $g_0$ and $\mathcal F_0$.

If $q_e=m$ and $q_m=0$, formulas 1.1–3.1 specialize to $M=q_e=m>0$, $x^0=T/\lambda$, $r=m+\lambda R$ and $\mathcal F_\lambda=-m(m+\lambda R)^{-2}dT\wedge dR$. These are exactly the current hypotheses and field pullback in [F2]; the same metric formula and local all-derivative convergence agree with that supplier. No statement about unprovided charge sectors is inferred from [F2].

derivations.claim:
For each integer $n\ge2$, choose $q_{e,n}=m\sqrt{1-n^{-2}}$ and $q_{m,n}=0$. By [F3], $Q_n^2=q_{e,n}^2=m^2(1-n^{-2})$, so $0<Q_n^2<m^2$ and $\sqrt{m^2-Q_n^2}=m/n$. Applying [F2] gives $r_{+,n}=m(1+1/n)$, $r_{-,n}=m(1-1/n)$, and
$$\kappa_{+,n}=\frac{r_{+,n}-r_{-,n}}{2r_{+,n}^2}=\frac{n}{m(n+1)^2},\qquad 0<\kappa_{+,n}<\frac1{mn}.$$

Let $c>0$ be any proposed inverse-length lower bound. Since $mc>0$, [F4]–[F5] allow a natural $N\ge1$ with $1/N<mc$. For every integer $n\ge2N$, $1/n\le1/(2N)<mc$, so step 1.1 gives $0<\kappa_{+,n}<1/(mn)<c$. Thus the sequence $\kappa_{+,n}$ tends to zero through subextremal RN data, contradicting any positive uniform lower bound. Every member of the sequence remains subextremal; only its limit reaches $Q^2=m^2$.
